name: Botulinum toxin type A
route_note: Local intramuscular injection; also intradermal (hyperhidrosis) and intradetrusor (bladder) injection. Units are not interchangeable between products.
originator: Alan B. Scott, Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute (therapeutic use); Allergan (Botox)

discovery.note: Identified Clostridium botulinum as the cause of botulism; Alan Scott pioneered therapeutic injection of the purified toxin for strabismus in the 1970s.

tagline: The most potent known toxin, used in tiny doses for spasticity, migraine and wrinkles
summary: Botulinum toxin type A is a bacterial neurotoxin that blocks acetylcholine release at nerve terminals, causing local, temporary muscle weakness. Several products are used for dystonia, spasticity, chronic migraine, overactive bladder, hyperhidrosis and cosmetic facial lines.
mechanism: The toxin's heavy chain binds gangliosides and the synaptic vesicle protein SV2 on cholinergic nerve terminals and is taken up by endocytosis. Its light chain, a zinc metalloprotease, is released into the cytosol and cleaves SNAP-25, a SNARE protein required for vesicle fusion.

Acetylcholine release is blocked for about three to four months until nerve terminals sprout and SNAP-25 is replenished. Effects on sensory neuropeptide release (such as CGRP) are proposed to explain benefit in chronic migraine.
uses: Overactive bladder and neurogenic detrusor overactivity
Temporary improvement of glabellar and other facial lines

history.title: Sausage poisoning
history.detail: Justinus Kerner describes botulism ('sausage poisoning') in detail and speculates on therapeutic use.

history.title: Bacterium identified
history.detail: Émile van Ermengem isolates Clostridium botulinum after a botulism outbreak in Belgium.

history.title: Purification
history.detail: Edward Schantz purifies crystalline type A toxin at Fort Detrick, later supplying it to researchers.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Alan Scott's Oculinum is approved for strabismus and blepharospasm; Allergan acquires it and renames it Botox.

history.title: Cosmetic use
history.detail: Botox Cosmetic is approved for glabellar lines.

history.title: Boxed warning
history.detail: The FDA requires a boxed warning on distant spread of toxin effect and assigns distinct non-proprietary names to products.

history.title: Chronic migraine
history.detail: The FDA approves onabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine prophylaxis.

history.title: AbbVie acquires Allergan
history.detail: AbbVie completes its roughly $63 billion acquisition of Allergan, owner of Botox.

history.title: Daxxify
history.detail: A longer-acting daxibotulinumtoxinA product is approved in the US.

pk.half_life: acts locally; clinical effect lasts about 3–4 months
pk.bioavailability: not systemically absorbed in meaningful amounts at therapeutic doses

common: Local muscle weakness (e.g. ptosis, neck weakness)
Urinary tract infection and retention (bladder use)
serious: Distant spread causing dysphagia, breathing difficulty and generalised weakness
safety.boxed_warning: Distant spread of toxin effect: symptoms of botulism (swallowing and breathing difficulty, generalised weakness) can occur hours to weeks after injection, and can be life-threatening.

facts: Botulinum toxin is the most lethal substance known; therapeutic doses are measured in nanograms.
Different botulinum toxin products are measured in proprietary units that cannot be converted between brands.
